question.content: I have gift card balances at several grocery delivery stores. I want to buy everything on my shopping list while spending as little cash out-of-pocket as possible. Each store I order from charges a delivery fee on top of item prices. A gift card covers part or all of a store's total (items + delivery fee); any remainder is out-of-pocket. Unused gift card balance simply stays on the card. Note that not every store carries every item. Figure out the best assignment of each item to a store and return a JSON object with keys: total_out_of_pocket (float), assignments (list of objects each with store_id, store_name, items (list of item names), item_cost, delivery_fee, store_total, gift_card_applied, out_of_pocket).

I need to get every item on my shopping list delivered, but no single store carries everything. Each store I order from charges a separate delivery fee. Find the smallest group of stores that together stock every item on my list. If there are ties in the number of stores, pick the group with the lowest total delivery fee. For each store in the group, list which items I should buy there. Return a JSON object with keys: num_stores (int), stores (list of objects each with store_id, store_name, items (list of item names), and delivery_fee), and total_delivery_fee (float).

I want to buy everything on my shopping list. Compare two options: (A) ordering everything from whichever single store gives me the lowest total cost including item prices, delivery fee, and service fee; versus (B) splitting my order across exactly three stores to minimize the combined total cost (item prices + all three delivery fees + all three service fees). Each store's service fee is computed as service_fee_rate times the item subtotal for that store. If no single store carries every item on the list, set best_single to null and cheaper_option to 'split'. Tell me the cost breakdown for each option and which is cheaper overall. Return a JSON object with keys: best_single (object with store_id, store_name, item_total, service_fee, delivery_fee, grand_total — or null if no single store carries everything), best_split (object with store_a, store_b, and store_c each containing store_id, store_name, items (list of item names), item_total, service_fee, delivery_fee, subtotal, plus a combined_total), and cheaper_option (string: 'single' or 'split').

My friends and I are choosing between six restaurants for dinner tonight. Return a JSON with keys: restaurant_name, business_id, costs (an object mapping each person — 'me', 'Mia', 'Jake' — to their individual Uber cost), and total_combined_cost.

My friend and I are coming from different neighborhoods and want to meet for dinner at whichever restaurant minimizes our total Uber cost. I'm at 742 Evergreen Terrace, San Francisco, CA and my friend is at 1234 Broadway, Oakland, CA. We're considering these five restaurants: Bella Vista, Lake Chalet, Chez Panisse, Burma Superstar, and Grocery Cafe. For each restaurant, get the Uber cost estimate from both of our locations to the restaurant, then tell us which one has the lowest combined cost. Return a JSON object with keys: restaurant_name, business_id, my_uber_cost, friend_uber_cost, total_combined_cost.

Look through the org chart history and tell me which manager has supervised the largest number of different employees overall. Count someone only once under the same manager, even if they reported to them during multiple periods. Respond with a JSON object with keys manager_id, manager_name, and unique_employee_count.

Look through this project history and tell me which person has worked with the largest number of different teammates overall. Two people are teammates if they reported to the same manager during overlapping time periods. Count each teammate only once, even if the overlap occurred under multiple managers or across multiple intervals. Respond with a JSON object with keys employee_id, employee_name, and unique_teammate_count.

Schedule four 30-minute one-on-ones for me with Alice, Bob, Charlie, and Diana next week. Use the minimum number of days, and among those schedules minimize the total idle time between consecutive meetings on the same day. If there is still a tie, choose the schedule whose first meeting starts earliest. Check everyone's calendars, find the best arrangement, and book all four meetings.

Next week, give a possible 45-minute meeting time for Alice, Bob, Charlie, Diana, and Eric. Each person may only meet between 10 a.m. and 3 p.m. local time on their own calendar, and you should prefer times with the fewest conflicts against their existing events. Reply with the proposed meeting start and end in UTC using ISO 8601 (with Z).

Look at my calendar for the next four weeks and tell me which day of the week tends to have the most fragmented free time — that is, the most separate free-time gaps between meetings during a standard 9 AM – 5 PM workday. Respond with a JSON object with keys day_of_week (e.g. "Monday"), total_free_blocks (summed across all instances of that weekday), and avg_free_blocks_per_day (rounded to one decimal place).

All original attendees must remain available at the new time. Find the best alternative time slot and book it.

Planning a friend's birthday and I really don't want to risk a bad pick. Help me find a SAFE BET. Try in this order:
  1. STRICT tier: business.rating >= 4.5 AND business.review_count >= 8 AND mean review rating across reviews with created_at >= 2026-01-27 is also >= 4.5. If multiple match, pick the one whose recent (last-90-day) reviews have the highest sum of useful_count. Tie-break by name ascending.
  2. RELAXED tier: same construction but with rating >= 4.0 and recent mean >= 4.0. Same tiebreaker.
  3. NONE: if nothing meets the relaxed criteria either, return tier="none" and pick=null.

A business needs at least one recent review (created_at >= 2026-01-27) to be considered in either tier; otherwise its recent_rating is undefined and it does not qualify.

Respond with JSON:
- tier: one of "strict", "relaxed", "none".
- pick: {business_id, name, rating, review_count, recent_rating, recent_useful_sum} or null. recent_rating rounded to 4 decimals. recent_useful_sum is the sum of useful_count across the recent reviews.
